note: Reference layer. A "wine" here is a named wine — an appellation, a protected denomination (AOC, DOCG, DO, AVA, GI, WO, PDO) or a classic style. Individual producer labels are not enumerable.

countries.name: Albania
countries.note: Ancient viticulture, small modern industry; Kallmet and the two Shesh grapes.

countries.name: Algeria
countries.note: Once the world's largest wine exporter under French rule; a fraction of that today.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.note: Malbec at altitude. The Uco Valley's high-elevation sites are the current frontier.

countries.name: Armenia
countries.note: Areni Noir from Vayots Dzor, near the world's oldest known winery site (c. 4100 BC).

countries.name: Australia
countries.note: Sixth-largest producer. Shiraz is the signature, and Rutherglen fortifieds are world-class rarities.

countries.name: Austria
countries.note: Grüner Veltliner and Blaufränkisch, plus Burgenland's botrytis sweet wines. Its DAC system is origin-typicity based.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
countries.note: Madrasa and Bayanshira on the Caspian side of the Caucasus.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.note: Small but growing, mostly Germanic white varieties and Crémant.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.note: Some of the highest vineyards on earth, above 2,000 m in Tarija.

countries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
countries.note: Žilavka and Blatina in the Herzegovina limestone.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.note: Sparkling wine is the strength; Vale do São Francisco harvests twice a year in the tropics.

countries.name: Bulgaria
countries.note: Mavrud and Melnik natives alongside a large Cabernet/Merlot export trade.

countries.name: Canada
countries.note: Icewine is the signature export; Okanagan and Niagara are the quality centres.

countries.name: Chile
countries.note: Phylloxera-free, geographically isolated, and the only real home of Carmenère.

countries.name: China
countries.note: Now among the largest vineyard areas in the world; Ningxia is the quality centre.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.note: Near-equatorial viticulture with two harvests a year.

countries.name: Croatia
countries.note: Plavac Mali on the Dalmatian coast; Zinfandel's ancestor Crljenak Kaštelanski originates here.

countries.name: Cyprus
countries.note: Commandaria has documented lineage to the Crusades and is claimed as the world's oldest named wine.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.note: Moravia does the bulk of it — Austrian in style, with Pálava as a local creation.

countries.name: Denmark
countries.note: Recognized as a wine-producing country by the EU in 2000; Solaris leads.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.note: Chota Valley, a rare equatorial wine zone.

countries.name: Egypt
countries.note: Winemaking documented to the Pharaohs; today a very small commercial industry.

countries.name: Ethiopia
countries.note: Rift Valley plantings, a recent and deliberate investment.

countries.name: France
countries.note: The reference point. Terroir-first, place-named rather than grape-named, and the source of the appellation model most of the world copied.

countries.name: Georgia
countries.note: The oldest continuous winemaking tradition known — roughly 8,000 years — and the qvevri amber-wine method.

countries.name: Germany
countries.note: Riesling's homeland. Classification runs on ripeness (Prädikat) alongside the newer vineyard-based VDP hierarchy.

countries.name: Greece
countries.note: Ancient roots, modern revival. Assyrtiko, Xinomavro and Agiorgitiko now travel internationally.

countries.name: Hungary
countries.note: Tokaji is the historic peak — the first classified vineyard region in the world (1737).

countries.name: India
countries.note: Nashik dominates; the industry is barely three decades old.

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.note: Bali produces year-round with no dormancy — up to three harvests annually.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.note: A handful of vineyards; maritime climate makes it marginal.

countries.name: Israel
countries.note: Modern quality era began in the 1980s in Galilee and the Golan.

countries.name: Italy
countries.note: The most grape-diverse country on earth — over 350 authorized native varieties, and nearly every one of its twenty regions makes wine.

countries.name: Japan
countries.note: Koshu is the native white and the country's identity grape.

countries.name: Jordan
countries.note: A small industry around Mount Nebo and the northern highlands.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.note: Assa Valley near Almaty, on old Soviet-era plantings.

countries.name: Kenya
countries.note: Naivasha near Lake Naivasha, at altitude on the equator.

countries.name: Kosovo
countries.note: Rahovec is the historic centre, once a major bulk supplier.

countries.name: Kyrgyzstan
countries.note: Chüy Valley, very small scale.

countries.name: Lebanon
countries.note: Bekaa Valley wine has survived war continuously; Château Musar is the international name.

countries.name: Luxembourg
countries.note: A small Moselle strip: Riesling, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, and a serious Crémant.

countries.name: Madagascar
countries.note: Highland vineyards near Fianarantsoa, mostly hybrids.

countries.name: Malta
countries.note: Two small islands, two native grapes: Ġellewża and Girgentina.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.note: The oldest wine industry in the Americas (1597); Valle de Guadalupe drives the modern revival.

countries.name: Moldova
countries.note: Enormous vineyard area per capita; Purcari's reds are the flagship.

countries.name: Montenegro
countries.note: Vranac from around Lake Skadar, largely from one very large producer.

countries.name: Morocco
countries.note: The largest wine industry in the Maghreb, mostly reds and the pale Gris de Boulaouane.

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.note: Two estates in Shan State at around 1,300 m.

countries.name: Namibia
countries.note: Desert-edge viticulture around Omaruru.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.note: A few hundred hectares of hybrids in the south, expanding with warming.

countries.name: New Zealand
countries.note: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc changed the global market in a single generation.

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.note: Vranec-dominated; historically the wine cellar of Yugoslavia.

countries.name: Norway
countries.note: Among the northernmost vineyards in the world, at roughly 59°N.

countries.name: Palestine
countries.note: Cremisan near Bethlehem works with indigenous Levantine varieties.

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.note: Small production, mostly Tannat and hybrids.

countries.name: Peru
countries.note: Mostly feeds pisco production, but Ica makes still wine too.

countries.name: Poland
countries.note: A genuinely new industry built on cold-hardy hybrids as the climate shifts.

countries.name: Portugal
countries.note: Two fortified wines of global rank (Port, Madeira) and a native-grape catalogue almost entirely its own.

countries.name: Romania
countries.note: One of Europe's largest producers by volume, with native Feteascăs and the sweet Cotnari tradition.

countries.name: Russia
countries.note: Krasnodar and the Black Sea coast, with Abrau-Dyurso the historic sparkling house.

countries.name: Serbia
countries.note: Prokupac-led revival plus Fruška Gora whites and the aromatized Bermet.

countries.name: Slovakia
countries.note: Shares the Tokaj region with Hungary; Small Carpathians is the main belt.

countries.name: Slovenia
countries.note: Three distinct zones; Brda's Rebula and orange wines share a border and a style with Friuli.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.note: Wine since 1659. Old-vine Chenin Blanc and the Swartland movement define the modern era.

countries.name: South Korea
countries.note: Campbell Early dominates; small but established.

countries.name: Spain
countries.note: Third-largest producer, largest vineyard area. Tempranillo and Garnacha at the core, plus sherry, the world's most underpriced fine wine.

countries.name: Sweden
countries.note: Skåne in the far south; disease-resistant hybrids, tiny volumes.

countries.name: Switzerland
countries.note: Drinks nearly all of it domestically. Chasselas in the west, Merlot in Ticino, and rare alpine natives in the Valais.

countries.name: Syria
countries.note: Bargylus in the Latakia hills continued production through the war.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.note: Subtropical viticulture in Changhua, two harvests per year.

countries.name: Tajikistan
countries.note: Sughd region, mostly sweet wines.

countries.name: Tanzania
countries.note: Dodoma has produced wine since the 1930s, originally by missionaries.

countries.name: Thailand
countries.note: The original New Latitude wine country, at 14°N with a managed dormancy cycle.

countries.name: Tunisia
countries.note: Muscat de Kelibia is the distinctive one; industry is small and coastal.

countries.name: Turkey
countries.note: Fourth-largest vineyard area globally, though most grapes go to table and drying.

countries.name: Turkmenistan
countries.note: State-run production with fortified styles from Terbash.

countries.name: Ukraine
countries.note: Odesa sparkling and Zakarpattia whites; Crimean production is under occupation.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.note: Traditional-method sparkling on the same chalk as Champagne — now the country's calling card.

countries.name: United States
countries.note: Fourth-largest producer. California is roughly 80 percent of it, but all 50 states now make wine.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.note: Tannat is the national grape, softer here than in its native Madiran.

countries.name: Uzbekistan
countries.note: Long Silk Road grape history; mostly sweet and fortified styles.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.note: Carora in Lara state, tropical and irrigated.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.note: Da Lat highlands; mostly table-grape derived.

countries.name: Zimbabwe
countries.note: A small industry, disrupted by land reform.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.note: Late-ripening and structured; the "Barolo of the south".

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.note: Once the single most planted wine grape on earth, almost all of it in one country.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.note: The same grape as Portugal's Alvarinho, across the river.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.note: A teinturier: red flesh, not just red skin.

grapes.name: Alphonse Lavallée
grapes.note: A table grape vinified in Bali.

grapes.name: Areni Noir
grapes.note: Grown beside the world's oldest known winery, dated to about 4100 BC.

grapes.name: Assyrtiko
grapes.note: Holds searing acidity in volcanic heat.

grapes.name: Auxerrois
grapes.note: A different grape from Malbec, confusingly also called Auxerrois in Cahors.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.note: Silvaner x Riesling crossed with Müller-Thurgau; England's aromatic white.

grapes.name: Blatina
grapes.note: Female-flowered; needs a pollinator variety.

grapes.name: Blauer Portugieser
grapes.note: A separate variety from Blaufränkisch despite the shared vineyards.

grapes.name: Blauer Wildbacher
grapes.note: The Schilcher grape.

grapes.name: Boğazkere
grapes.note: Tannic enough that it is almost always blended with Öküzgözü.

grapes.name: Bonarda Argentina
grapes.note: Argentina's second-most planted red; unrelated to Italy's Bonarda.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: Parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Carmenère.

grapes.name: Cabernet Gernischt
grapes.note: Long grown in China; DNA suggests it is Carmenère.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: A chance Cabernet Franc x Sauvignon Blanc crossing; now the most planted wine grape on earth.

grapes.name: Campbell Early
grapes.note: Labrusca hybrid; the mainstay of Korean wine.

grapes.name: Cardinal
grapes.note: A table grape used for wine in Southeast Asia.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.note: Nearly lost in France; found in Chile in 1994 after decades misidentified as Merlot.

grapes.name: Chambourcin
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Neutral enough to transmit site and winemaking rather than itself.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.note: Makes bone-dry, sparkling and botrytis sweet wine from the same vineyard.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: A parent of Pinotage.

grapes.name: Concord
grapes.note: Vitis labrusca; the flavour most Americans call "grape".

grapes.name: Couderc
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Croatina
grapes.note: Italy's Bonarda; unrelated to Argentina's.

grapes.name: Delaware
grapes.note: Vitis labrusca hybrid, widely grown in Japan.

grapes.name: Elbling
grapes.note: One of the oldest varieties on the Mosel.

grapes.name: Fetească Regală
grapes.note: A 20th-century Fetească Albă x Grasă crossing.

grapes.name: Freisa
grapes.note: A close relative of Nebbiolo.

grapes.name: Frontenac
grapes.note: Cold-hardy hybrid bred in Minnesota.

grapes.name: Frühburgunder
grapes.note: Early-ripening mutation of Pinot Noir.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.note: The Tokaji grape; botrytis-prone and fiercely acidic.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.note: Banished from Burgundy by decree in 1395; found its home in Beaujolais.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.note: The Soave grape.

grapes.name: Gewurztraminer
grapes.note: Aromatic pink-berried mutation of Savagnin.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.note: Renamed in 2009 so that Prosecco could become a protected place name.

grapes.name: Grasă de Cotnari
grapes.note: Botrytis-prone; the Cotnari sweet-wine grape.

grapes.name: Grk
grapes.note: Female-flowered; must be interplanted with another variety to fruit.

grapes.name: Hibernal
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Hondarrabi Zuri
grapes.note: The Txakoli grape.

grapes.name: Italia
grapes.note: A table grape (Bicane x Muscat Hamburg) vinified in Peru.

grapes.name: Johanniter
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.note: Bulgaria grows the same grape as Gamza.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.note: Trollinger x Riesling.

grapes.name: Koshu
grapes.note: Pink-skinned, vinified white; carried to Japan along the Silk Road.

grapes.name: L'Acadie Blanc
grapes.note: Bred in Ontario; Nova Scotia's signature white.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.note: Left Bordeaux for Argentina and became someone else's national grape.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.note: A family of related varieties, not one grape.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.note: Cabernet Sauvignon x Grenache, bred 1961; now China's calling card.

grapes.name: Mavro
grapes.note: Cyprus's most planted variety.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.note: The Jaen of Portugal's Dão is the same grape.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: The world's second-most planted red; early-ripening and supple.

grapes.name: Monemvasia
grapes.note: The probable origin of the name Malvasia.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.note: A grape, not the Tuscan town of the same name.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.note: Riesling x Madeleine Royale, bred 1882.

grapes.name: Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge
grapes.note: Red-berried mutation; the Rutherglen Muscat grape.

grapes.name: Muscat Bailey A
grapes.note: Bailey x Muscat Hamburg, bred in Japan in 1927.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
grapes.note: The oldest domesticated wine grape still in wide use.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.note: Pale, tannic and long-lived — Barolo and Barbaresco are both this grape.

grapes.name: Negramoll
grapes.note: Madeira's Tinta Negra is generally held to be the same variety.

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese
grapes.note: Etna's red; often compared to Nebbiolo for its perfume and tannin.

grapes.name: Norton
grapes.note: A Vitis aestivalis hybrid; the backbone of 19th-century Missouri wine.

grapes.name: País
grapes.note: The first vinifera grape planted in the Americas, in the 1500s.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.note: The sherry grape; neutral by nature, transformed entirely by flor and oxidation.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris
grapes.note: Pink-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, vinified as white.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Thin-skinned and site-sensitive; the reason Burgundy is mapped vineyard by vineyard.

grapes.name: Pinotage
grapes.note: Pinot Noir x Cinsault, bred in 1925 at Stellenbosch.

grapes.name: Plavac Mali
grapes.note: An offspring of Zinfandel and Dobričić.

grapes.name: Quebranta
grapes.note: A País x Negramoll crossing; mostly distilled into pisco.

grapes.name: Ramisco
grapes.note: Grown ungrafted in deep sand, which phylloxera cannot cross.

grapes.name: Regent
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Ribolla Gialla
grapes.note: A cornerstone of the modern orange-wine movement.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: Holds acidity at any ripeness, which is why it ages for decades.

grapes.name: Rkatsiteli
grapes.note: One of the oldest cultivated varieties still in commercial use.

grapes.name: Romorantin
grapes.note: Grown almost nowhere but Cour-Cheverny.

grapes.name: Rondo
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Rubin
grapes.note: Nebbiolo x Syrah, bred in Bulgaria in 1944.

grapes.name: Ruby Cabernet
grapes.note: Cabernet Sauvignon x Carignan.

grapes.name: Ryzlink
grapes.note: Generic Czech term for Riesling-named varieties.

grapes.name: Sagrantino
grapes.note: Among the most tannic varieties measured anywhere.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.note: Italy's most planted grape; Corsica's Nielluccio is the same variety.

grapes.name: Saperavi
grapes.note: A teinturier with red flesh; Georgia's principal red.

grapes.name: Savagnin
grapes.note: The Vin Jaune grape, and ancestor of Gewürztraminer.

grapes.name: Savatiano
grapes.note: The Retsina grape and Greece's most planted variety.

grapes.name: Sciaccarello
grapes.note: Corsica's name for Tuscany's Mammolo.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.note: Botrytis-prone, which is exactly why Sauternes exists.

grapes.name: Sercial
grapes.note: The driest of the Madeira grapes.

grapes.name: Seyval Blanc
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Solaris
grapes.note: Hybrid bred for cold climates; the reason Scandinavia has vineyards.

grapes.name: Sultaniye
grapes.note: Sultana / Thompson Seedless, vinified in the Aegean.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: One grape, two names; the name signals intended style more than genetics.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: Uruguay's national grape, softer there than in its native Madiran.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.note: Spain's noble red, with a different name in nearly every region that grows it.

grapes.name: Terrano
grapes.note: Related to but distinct from Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso.

grapes.name: Terrantez
grapes.note: Nearly extinct; a few hectares survive.

grapes.name: Timorasso
grapes.note: Rescued from near-extinction in the 1980s.

grapes.name: Torrontés Riojano
grapes.note: A Muscat of Alexandria x País crossing born in Argentina.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.note: The most planted grape in the Douro.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.note: Portugal's flagship red, for Port and increasingly for table wine.

grapes.name: Traminac
grapes.note: Croatian name for Gewürztraminer.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.note: The base of both Vin Santo and Cognac.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.note: Genetically identical to the Veneto's Trebbiano di Soave.

grapes.name: Vidal
grapes.note: Hybrid; the workhorse of Canadian icewine.

grapes.name: Vignoles
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Villard
grapes.note: Hybrid.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.note: Down to about 14 hectares worldwide in the 1960s.

grapes.name: Welschriesling
grapes.note: No relation to Riesling despite the name.

grapes.name: Xinomavro
grapes.note: Pale, tannic and slow — Greece's answer to Nebbiolo.

grapes.name: Žametovka
grapes.note: Home to the world's oldest living grapevine, in Maribor.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.note: Zinfandel, Primitivo and Croatia's Tribidrag are one grape, settled by DNA in 2001.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.note: Blaufränkisch x St. Laurent, bred 1922; Austria's most planted red.

wines.n: Côtes de Provence Notre-Dame des Anges
Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva
Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
Green Valley of Russian River Valley
